terms.eli16: A computer chip designed specifically to run AI faster — like a specialized engine built just for AI calculations.

terms.definition: The research challenge of ensuring AI systems pursue goals consistent with human values and intentions. Misaligned AI might optimize for proxy goals in harmful ways.
terms.eli16: Making sure AI systems actually want what we want them to want — not finding harmful shortcuts.

terms.definition: Visual artwork created with AI systems, typically using diffusion models or GANs. AI art has sparked debates about creativity, authorship, and copyright.
terms.eli16: Images created by AI — you describe what you want and the AI generates the picture.

terms.definition: A problem is AI-complete if solving it computationally is as hard as solving the full problem of general AI — requiring human-level understanding.
terms.eli16: Problems so hard that solving them would basically require building a fully human-level AI.

terms.definition: Frameworks, policies, regulations, and institutions designed to guide responsible AI development and deployment, addressing safety, fairness, transparency, and accountability.
terms.eli16: The rules and guidelines governing how AI is built and used — like traffic laws but for artificial intelligence.

terms.definition: An organization's preparedness to adopt AI technologies effectively — encompassing data infrastructure, talent, processes, culture, and governance.
terms.eli16: How ready a company is to successfully use AI — whether they have the right data, people, tools, and mindset.

terms.definition: Intentionally attacking or probing an AI system to find vulnerabilities, failure modes, and potential harms before deployment — testing jailbreaks and adversarial inputs.
terms.eli16: Deliberately trying to break or trick an AI system to find its weaknesses before real users encounter them.

terms.definition: An interdisciplinary research field focused on ensuring AI systems behave safely and beneficially, covering technical problems like alignment and interpretability plus governance.
terms.eli16: The field dedicated to making sure AI systems don't cause harm — now or as they become more powerful.

terms.definition: Techniques for embedding detectable signals in AI-generated content (text, images, audio) to indicate AI origin, aiding content authenticity verification.
terms.eli16: Hidden signals in AI-created content so you can tell it was made by an AI — like an invisible stamp.

terms.definition: A period of reduced funding and progress in AI research following inflated expectations. Two major AI winters occurred in the 1970s and late 1980s.
terms.eli16: A slow period in AI history when funding dried up because the technology didn't live up to the hype.

terms.definition: The computational tasks involved in training, fine-tuning, or running inference on AI models — characterized by high parallelism, large memory requirements, and specialized hardware usage.
terms.eli16: The heavy-duty computing work involved in running or training AI models, requiring powerful specialized chips.

terms.definition: Applying AI and machine learning to automate IT operations — including anomaly detection, event correlation, root cause analysis, and automated remediation.
terms.eli16: Using AI to help manage and fix IT systems automatically — catching and resolving problems without human intervention.

terms.definition: A measure of computational resources (time and memory) required by an algorithm, typically expressed using Big O notation.
terms.eli16: How fast and resource-light an algorithm is — efficient algorithms get the same answer with less time and memory.

terms.definition: From algorithmic information theory: assigning probabilities to strings based on program lengths that generate them. Shorter programs mean higher probability, related to Occam's Razor.
terms.eli16: A mathematical way to assign probabilities to patterns — simpler patterns that can be described more briefly get higher probability.

terms.definition: The challenge of specifying and instilling correct values and objectives into AI systems so they behave as intended. Core concern in AI safety as systems become more capable.
terms.eli16: The fundamental challenge of getting AI to want the right things — ensuring powerful AI pursues goals truly good for humanity.

terms.definition: DeepMind's AI that defeated world champion Go players in 2016 using deep neural networks and Monte Carlo tree search. AlphaGo Zero later learned entirely from self-play.
terms.eli16: DeepMind's AI that beat the world's best human Go players in 2016 — a landmark moment in AI history.

terms.definition: Amazon Web Services' managed platform for building and scaling generative AI applications using foundation models from Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, and others without managing infrastructure.
terms.eli16: Amazon's cloud service for building AI apps using leading AI models, without having to manage servers.

terms.definition: Theoretical study of computational complexity of algorithms — how time and space requirements scale with input size. Basis for comparing and choosing algorithms.
terms.eli16: Mathematically figuring out how fast an algorithm runs and how much memory it uses as problems get bigger.

terms.definition: Systematic computational analysis of data to discover patterns and support decision-making. Includes descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analytics.
terms.eli16: Analyzing data to find patterns and insights that help you understand what happened and make better decisions.

terms.definition: A form of declarative programming for difficult search problems. Programs are expressed as logical rules and the system finds 'answer sets' — stable models satisfying all rules.
terms.eli16: A programming style where you describe the rules and the computer finds all valid solutions automatically.

terms.definition: A probabilistic optimization technique inspired by ant pheromone behavior. Ants leave trails that guide subsequent ants toward better paths — applied to routing and scheduling problems.
terms.eli16: An optimization algorithm inspired by how ants find the shortest path to food, applied to routing and scheduling.

terms.definition: An algorithm that can be interrupted at any point and still returns a valid, possibly suboptimal solution. Quality improves with more computation time — useful in real-time AI systems.
terms.eli16: An algorithm that gives a 'good enough' answer immediately and keeps improving it if given more time.

terms.definition: An open-source framework for distributed storage and processing of very large datasets across computer clusters using the MapReduce programming model.
terms.eli16: Software that lets you store and process massive amounts of data across many computers at once.

terms.definition: An open table format for large analytic datasets in data lakes, supporting ACID transactions, schema evolution, and time-travel queries on cloud storage.
terms.eli16: A smart system for organizing huge amounts of data in cloud storage, making updates and queries much easier.

terms.definition: An open-source distributed event streaming platform for high-throughput, fault-tolerant real-time data pipelines. Originally developed by LinkedIn.
terms.eli16: A high-speed conveyor belt for data — reliably moving huge amounts of real-time data between applications.

terms.definition: An open-source unified analytics engine for large-scale data processing with modules for streaming, SQL, machine learning, and graph processing. Much faster than Hadoop for many workloads.
terms.eli16: A fast engine for processing massive datasets across many computers, widely used for AI and big data tasks.

terms.definition: A computing environment providing infrastructure, services, and tools for developing, running, and managing applications — including middleware and runtime environments.
terms.eli16: The computing environment where apps run — providing all the underlying services and infrastructure they need.

terms.definition: Techniques for finding strings that approximately match a pattern, tolerating spelling errors, typos, or variations. Used in spell-checkers, search engines, and DNA sequencing.
terms.eli16: Searching for text that's close to what you're looking for, even if there are typos or slight differences.

terms.definition: The difference between an exact value and an approximation. In ML, the error introduced when a model uses a simplified representation instead of the true underlying function.
terms.eli16: The gap between a model's simplified answer and the true correct answer.

terms.definition: A formal model for representing arguments and their relationships (attack, support). Used in AI for knowledge representation, legal reasoning, and multi-agent systems.
terms.eli16: A formal way for AI to reason about conflicting arguments — mapping which arguments attack or support each other.

terms.definition: Processors using the ARM architecture, known for energy efficiency. Increasingly used in AI accelerators and edge devices; Apple Silicon and AWS Graviton use ARM.
terms.eli16: Energy-efficient computer chips used in phones, tablets, and increasingly in AI hardware — the architecture inside most mobile devices.

terms.definition: A computational intelligence system inspired by the vertebrate immune system's ability to detect and respond to pathogens. Used for anomaly detection, fault tolerance, and optimization.
terms.eli16: An AI system inspired by the human immune system — it learns to identify and respond to abnormal patterns.

terms.definition: A computing system loosely modeled on biological neural networks. Consists of interconnected nodes (neurons) organized in layers that learn patterns from data through weighted connections.
terms.eli16: A computer system inspired by the human brain, made of interconnected artificial neurons that learn patterns from examples.

terms.definition: A hypothetical form of AI that surpasses human intelligence across all domains — not just in specific tasks but in general reasoning, creativity, and problem-solving.
terms.eli16: A hypothetical future AI that would be smarter than the smartest human in every possible way.

terms.definition: Devices and software that help people with disabilities perform tasks that might otherwise be difficult or impossible. AI-powered assistive tech includes screen readers, speech recognition, and real-time captions.
terms.eli16: Technology that helps people with disabilities — like AI-powered captions, screen readers, or voice control.

terms.definition: A mathematical framework describing how an algorithm's resource requirements grow relative to input size, ignoring constant factors. The basis of Big O, Big Omega, and Big Theta notation.
terms.eli16: A way to describe how much slower an algorithm gets as problems get bigger — ignoring small constant differences.

terms.definition: The use of AI to enhance human decision-making and capabilities rather than replace human judgment. AI acts as a tool that amplifies human intelligence.
terms.eli16: AI designed to make humans smarter and more capable — not to replace them, but to enhance their abilities.

terms.definition: Technology that overlays digital information — images, text, or 3D objects — onto the real world, viewed through a device like a phone or headset. Used in gaming, navigation, and industrial applications.
terms.eli16: Digital information and visuals overlaid onto the real world through your phone or special glasses.

terms.definition: The study of abstract machines (automata) and the computational problems they can solve. Fundamental to understanding the limits of computation and the design of programming languages.
terms.eli16: The study of abstract machines — mathematical models that define what computers can and cannot compute.

terms.definition: An area of AI concerned with generating sequences of actions to achieve goals from an initial state, considering resource constraints and action effects.
terms.eli16: AI that figures out a sequence of steps to complete a goal, like planning the most efficient schedule for a robot.

terms.definition: The use of computers to perform logical reasoning and prove theorems automatically. Encompasses theorem proving, model checking, and constraint solving.
terms.eli16: Teaching computers to reason logically and prove mathematical statements automatically.

terms.definition: A computing approach where systems manage themselves — self-configuring, self-healing, self-optimizing, and self-protecting — inspired by the human autonomic nervous system.
terms.eli16: Computing systems that manage themselves automatically — fixing problems, adjusting settings, and optimizing performance without human intervention.

terms.definition: AI systems that can operate independently without ongoing human supervision, making decisions and taking actions to achieve goals in dynamic environments.
terms.eli16: AI that can work on its own without needing constant human supervision or direction.

terms.definition: A vehicle capable of sensing its environment and navigating without human input, using cameras, lidar, radar, and AI to detect obstacles and plan routes.
terms.eli16: A car that drives itself using cameras, sensors, and AI — no human needed to steer.

terms.definition: A robot that can perform behaviors or tasks with a high degree of independence from human supervision, using sensors and AI to perceive and act in its environment.
terms.eli16: A robot that can figure out what to do and do it without step-by-step human instructions.

terms.definition: An extension of backpropagation for training recurrent neural networks by unrolling the network through time steps and computing gradients across the sequence.
terms.eli16: The algorithm used to train RNNs by unfolding the network over time and computing how each past step contributed to errors.

terms.definition: An inference strategy in expert systems that starts from the goal and works backward to find supporting facts. Opposite of forward chaining.
terms.eli16: An AI reasoning method that starts from the desired conclusion and works backward to find what facts would prove it.

terms.definition: A probability theorem describing how to update beliefs based on new evidence: P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B). Foundation of Bayesian reasoning and many ML algorithms.
terms.eli16: A formula for updating your beliefs when you get new evidence — the basis of a lot of AI probability reasoning.

terms.definition: A programming approach based on Bayesian probability theory for writing probabilistic programs. Used for robot learning, signal processing, and AI systems that reason under uncertainty.
terms.eli16: A programming style based on probability theory, useful for building AI that can reason about uncertain information.

terms.definition: A modular, hierarchical control structure used in game AI and robotics to organize complex behaviors. More readable and maintainable than finite state machines for complex agents.
terms.eli16: A tree-shaped structure for organizing an AI character's or robot's behaviors — making complex decision-making easier to design and read.

terms.definition: Google's 2018 transformer model pre-trained on bidirectional context. BERT revolutionized NLP by learning deep language representations from unlabeled text, enabling transfer learning for many NLP tasks.
terms.eli16: Google's influential AI language model that reads text in both directions at once, revolutionizing how AI understands language.

terms.definition: A fundamental ML concept: reducing model bias (underfitting) typically increases variance (overfitting) and vice versa. Finding the right balance is key to building models that generalize well.
terms.eli16: The balancing act in ML between a model being too simple (missing patterns) and too complex (memorizing noise).

terms.definition: Mathematical notation describing the upper bound on an algorithm's time or space requirements as a function of input size, ignoring constant factors. O(n), O(n²), O(log n) are common examples.
terms.eli16: Shorthand for describing how much slower an algorithm gets as inputs grow — O(n) is linear, O(n²) is much worse.

terms.definition: Google Cloud's serverless, multi-cloud data warehouse designed for high-speed SQL analytics on massive datasets. Automatically scales compute resources and charges per query.
terms.eli16: Google's cloud database system for analyzing massive amounts of data quickly using regular SQL queries.

terms.definition: A storage system designed for unstructured data like images, videos, audio files, and documents. Cloud providers offer BLOB storage as scalable object storage services.
terms.eli16: Cloud storage for large files like images, videos, and documents — not structured data but raw binary files.

terms.definition: A tree data structure where each node has at most two children (left and right). Binary search trees maintain sorted order, enabling O(log n) search, insertion, and deletion.
terms.eli16: A data structure shaped like a family tree where each parent has at most two children — used to store and search data efficiently.

terms.definition: An AI problem-solving architecture where multiple specialized knowledge sources share a common data structure (the blackboard) and independently contribute to a solution.
terms.eli16: An AI architecture where multiple specialized experts share a common workspace and each contributes their part toward solving a problem.

terms.definition: A type of stochastic recurrent neural network that learns a probability distribution over inputs. Used as building blocks in deep learning architectures and for dimensionality reduction.
terms.eli16: A type of neural network that learns the underlying patterns in data by modeling their probability distribution.

terms.definition: The problem of determining if there exists an assignment of truth values to variables that makes a Boolean formula true. The first problem proven NP-complete; SAT solvers are widely used in AI.
terms.eli16: The classic hard problem of figuring out if there's a way to set true/false variables that makes a logical formula true.

terms.definition: An ensemble ML technique that combines many weak learners sequentially, with each new model focusing on correcting errors made by previous ones. XGBoost and LightGBM are popular implementations.
terms.eli16: An ML technique that trains many simple models in sequence, each fixing the mistakes of the previous one — together they form a powerful predictor.

terms.definition: An ensemble learning technique that trains multiple models on different random subsets of training data and combines predictions. Reduces variance and helps prevent overfitting.
terms.eli16: An ML technique that trains many models on different random samples of data and averages their predictions for better accuracy.

terms.definition: The number of children each node in a search tree has on average. A high branching factor makes exhaustive search exponentially more expensive.
terms.eli16: How many options branch off from each decision point in a search — higher branching factor makes the search much harder.

terms.definition: A problem-solving technique that systematically tries every possible solution until finding one that works. Guaranteed to find the answer but computationally expensive for large problems.
terms.eli16: Trying every possible solution one by one until you find one that works — reliable but slow for big problems.

terms.definition: Technologies, strategies, and processes that transform raw data into actionable insights for business decision-making. Includes dashboards, reporting, OLAP, and data visualization.
terms.eli16: Tools and processes that turn company data into useful charts and insights to help leaders make better decisions.

terms.definition: An AI problem-solving approach that retrieves and adapts solutions from similar past experiences (cases) to solve new problems. Used in expert systems and recommendation engines.
terms.eli16: An AI approach that solves new problems by finding similar past situations and adapting their solutions.

terms.definition: The process of organizing items into groups based on shared characteristics. In information science, category trees provide hierarchical organization of concepts.
terms.eli16: Organizing things into groups and hierarchies based on their shared characteristics.

terms.definition: A database technique that tracks and captures all changes (inserts, updates, deletes) made to data in real time, enabling downstream systems to react to data changes.
terms.eli16: Technology that watches a database for any changes and immediately notifies other systems — like a live feed of all data updates.

terms.definition: OpenAI's enterprise-grade version of ChatGPT, offering enhanced privacy (no data training), unlimited GPT-4 access, advanced data analysis, custom GPTs, admin controls, and SSO integration.
terms.eli16: The business version of ChatGPT with enhanced privacy, no data sharing, and admin controls for companies.

terms.definition: OpenAI's model that learns visual concepts from natural language descriptions by training on image-text pairs. Enables zero-shot image classification and powers many image generation models.
terms.eli16: An AI model that understands both images and text together — trained by matching millions of images to their descriptions.

terms.definition: The design of cloud computing systems including the components, services, infrastructure, and relationships needed to meet technical and business requirements in a cloud environment.
terms.eli16: The blueprint for how a cloud computing system is designed — what components it has and how they connect.

terms.definition: A hybrid cloud deployment model where an application runs on private cloud or on-premises infrastructure and 'bursts' to public cloud resources when demand exceeds local capacity.
terms.eli16: A setup where your app normally runs on your own servers but automatically switches to rented cloud servers when traffic spikes.

terms.definition: The ability of a cloud system to automatically scale resources up or down in response to changing workload demands, paying only for what's used.
terms.eli16: Cloud computing's ability to automatically grow or shrink resources to match demand — like a balloon that inflates and deflates.

terms.definition: A financial operations discipline for managing cloud costs. Teams collaborate to optimize cloud spending, balance cost with performance, and increase business value from cloud investments.
terms.eli16: The practice of managing and optimizing how much you spend on cloud services — making sure cloud money is well spent.

terms.definition: An approach to building and running applications that fully exploits the advantages of cloud computing — using microservices, containers, dynamic orchestration, and DevOps practices.
terms.eli16: Building applications designed from the ground up to run in the cloud, using modern patterns like containers and microservices.

terms.definition: A field of robotics that uses cloud computing to enhance robot capabilities — offloading heavy computation to the cloud, enabling knowledge sharing between robots, and remote monitoring.
terms.eli16: Robots that use cloud computing for heavy thinking — the robot handles the physical work, the cloud handles complex calculations.

terms.definition: The ability of a cloud system to handle growing workloads by adding resources (scaling up or out) or reducing resources when demand decreases, maintaining performance and reliability.
terms.eli16: A cloud system's ability to grow to handle more work and shrink back down when demand drops.

terms.definition: An unsupervised ML technique that groups similar data points together based on their features, without predefined labels. Used in customer segmentation, anomaly detection, and data exploration.
terms.eli16: An AI technique that automatically groups similar data points together without being told what the groups should be.

terms.definition: A blueprint for designing intelligent systems based on theories of human cognition. Examples: ACT-R, SOAR. Specifies how perception, memory, learning, and action are organized.
terms.eli16: A detailed blueprint for building AI based on theories of how the human mind works.

terms.definition: Creating computational models that simulate human cognitive processes — memory, attention, decision-making, learning — to understand and predict human behavior.
terms.eli16: Building computer models that simulate how humans think, remember, and make decisions.

terms.definition: An interdisciplinary field studying the mind and intelligence, spanning psychology, neuroscience, linguistics, philosophy, and AI. Aims to understand how minds think, learn, and perceive.
terms.eli16: The study of how minds work — combining psychology, neuroscience, linguistics, and AI to understand intelligence.

terms.definition: Enterprise search technology that uses AI — NLP, machine learning, knowledge graphs — to understand intent and context, delivering more relevant results than keyword search.
terms.eli16: AI-powered search that understands what you mean, not just what you typed — like having a smart assistant find information for you.

terms.definition: Finding the best solution from a finite but very large set of possible solutions. Problems include the travelling salesman problem and scheduling. Often NP-hard, requiring heuristics or approximate algorithms.
terms.eli16: Finding the best arrangement or selection from a huge number of possibilities — like finding the shortest route visiting many cities.

terms.definition: The large body of basic facts about the world that humans take for granted — physical properties, social norms, cause-and-effect. A long-standing challenge for AI to acquire and use effectively.
terms.eli16: All the basic 'obvious' knowledge about the world that humans take for granted but AI systems struggle to learn.

terms.definition: The ability to apply everyday knowledge about the world to interpret situations and make inferences. A major challenge in AI — systems often lack the implicit understanding humans use constantly.
terms.eli16: The AI ability to reason with everyday, obvious knowledge — understanding that fire is hot or that people need sleep.

terms.definition: The computational resources — processing power, memory, and storage — required to train or run AI models. Access to compute is a key bottleneck in AI development.
terms.eli16: The processing power and hardware resources needed to train and run AI models — a critical constraint in AI development.

terms.definition: A branch of computer science studying the resources (time, memory) needed to solve computational problems. Classifies problems by difficulty into classes like P, NP, and PSPACE.
terms.eli16: The study of how hard different computational problems are and how to classify them by difficulty.

terms.definition: The study and development of AI systems that exhibit behavior deemed creative in humans — generating art, music, poetry, or novel scientific hypotheses.
terms.eli16: AI that can generate creative outputs like art, music, or stories — the study of machine creativity.

terms.definition: An interdisciplinary field that uses mathematical models and theoretical analysis to understand how the nervous system processes information and produces behavior.
terms.eli16: Using math and computer models to understand how the brain processes information and controls behavior.

terms.definition: The study of computation, algorithms, data structures, programming languages, and the design of computing systems. Encompasses both theoretical foundations and practical engineering.
terms.eli16: The study of how computers work, how to program them, and how to solve problems using algorithms and data structures.

terms.definition: The phenomenon where the statistical properties of the target variable that a model predicts change over time, causing model performance to degrade. Requires continuous model monitoring and retraining.
terms.eli16: When the real world changes and your AI model's predictions become less accurate because it was trained on outdated data.

terms.definition: A theoretical approach in cognitive science and AI that models mental phenomena using networks of simple, interconnected units — the theoretical foundation of neural networks and deep learning.
terms.eli16: The theory that intelligence emerges from large networks of simple connected units — the foundation behind neural networks.

terms.definition: A programming paradigm for solving combinatorial problems by declaring constraints that solutions must satisfy. A constraint solver finds assignments that satisfy all constraints.
terms.eli16: A way of solving problems by describing what rules the solution must follow, and letting the computer find a valid solution.

terms.definition: A language deliberately created by a person or organization rather than naturally evolved — like Esperanto, Klingon, or Lojban. AI language models can learn and generate constructed languages.
terms.eli16: A language invented on purpose rather than evolving naturally — like Esperanto or the fictional languages in Star Trek.

terms.definition: Lightweight, portable packages that bundle an application with its dependencies and configuration, running consistently across different computing environments. Docker is the most popular container format.
terms.eli16: Lightweight packages that wrap an application and everything it needs to run, so it works the same on any computer.

terms.definition: The practice of carefully designing and managing the information provided to an LLM in its context window to optimize output quality — including system prompts, examples, retrieved documents, and conversation history.
terms.eli16: The art of carefully crafting what information you give an AI model so it performs at its best.

terms.definition: A branch of mathematics and engineering that deals with influencing the behavior of dynamical systems. Forms the basis for autopilots, thermostats, and reinforcement learning.
terms.eli16: The mathematical study of how to steer or control systems — used in everything from thermostats to aircraft autopilots.

terms.definition: Facebook's AI Go-playing program, a precursor to AlphaGo using deep convolutional neural networks. Demonstrated that deep learning could achieve strong Go play before DeepMind's breakthrough.
terms.eli16: Facebook's AI Go player from 2015 — an early demonstration that deep learning could tackle complex strategy games.

terms.definition: The 1956 summer research project at Dartmouth College that coined the term 'artificial intelligence' and is considered the founding event of AI as an academic discipline.
terms.eli16: The 1956 workshop where 'artificial intelligence' was coined and the field was officially founded — the birthplace of AI.

terms.definition: A cloud architecture where data is centralized, governed, and accessible across an organization's cloud environments, enabling data sharing and analytics at scale.
terms.eli16: A unified cloud environment where all of an organization's data is stored, managed, and accessed from one place.

terms.definition: A framework proposing that individuals should have rights and potentially compensation for the data they generate, which is used to train AI systems. Advocates like Jaron Lanier support this concept.
terms.eli16: The idea that people should have rights over the data they create and potentially be paid when it's used to train AI.

terms.definition: The process of integrating data from multiple sources to produce more accurate and comprehensive information than any single source provides. Used in sensor fusion, military intelligence, and analytics.
terms.eli16: Combining data from multiple sources to get a more complete and accurate picture than any single source could provide.

terms.definition: The set of policies, processes, and standards for managing data assets across an organization — ensuring data quality, security, privacy, and regulatory compliance.
terms.eli16: The rules and processes an organization uses to manage its data responsibly — ensuring it's accurate, secure, and properly used.

terms.definition: The process of importing, collecting, and loading data from various sources into a storage system for processing or analysis. Can be batch-based or real-time streaming.
terms.eli16: The process of collecting and loading data from various sources into a system where it can be processed and analyzed.

terms.definition: Combining data from different sources into a unified view, resolving differences in format, structure, and meaning. Foundational for analytics and AI systems that rely on multiple data sources.
terms.eli16: Combining data from different systems into one consistent, unified dataset that can be analyzed together.

terms.definition: The process of tagging, annotating, or categorizing raw data (images, text, audio) to create training datasets for supervised machine learning models.
terms.eli16: Adding labels to raw data — like telling an AI 'this image is a cat' — so it can learn from examples.

terms.definition: A centralized repository that stores raw data in its native format at any scale — structured, semi-structured, and unstructured. Data is transformed when needed rather than on ingestion.
terms.eli16: A giant storage pool that holds all kinds of raw data in any format, ready to be processed and analyzed later.

terms.definition: The tracking of data's origin, movement, and transformation throughout its lifecycle — where it came from, how it changed, and where it went. Essential for debugging, compliance, and trust.
terms.eli16: The ability to trace where data came from, how it was changed, and where it went — like a family tree for your data.

terms.definition: A decentralized data architecture approach where domain teams own and serve their own data as products, rather than having a centralized data team. Aims to scale data access across large organizations.
terms.eli16: A modern approach to data management where each team owns their own data and makes it available as a product for others.

terms.definition: Collecting, organizing, and transforming raw data into useful information through operations like filtering, aggregation, classification, and computation.
terms.eli16: Taking raw data and turning it into something useful through sorting, calculating, and organizing.

terms.definition: A centralized repository for storing structured, cleaned, and processed data from multiple sources, optimized for analytical queries and business reporting.
terms.eli16: A large organized database that stores cleaned, historical data from across a company for analysis and reporting.

terms.definition: In classification, the boundary in feature space that separates data points assigned to different classes. The shape of the decision boundary depends on the model type.
terms.eli16: The imaginary line (or surface) that an ML model draws between different categories — points on one side are classified differently from points on the other.

terms.definition: An information system that supports business or organizational decision-making activities. DSS combines data analysis, models, and user interface to help analyze complex situations.
terms.eli16: Software that helps leaders make better decisions by organizing relevant information and running analyses.

terms.definition: A supervised ML method that builds a tree-like model of decisions based on feature values. Each internal node represents a feature test, branches represent outcomes, and leaves represent class labels.
terms.eli16: An ML model that makes predictions by asking a series of yes/no questions — like a flowchart that classifies things.

terms.definition: A programming paradigm that expresses what the program should accomplish rather than how to accomplish it. SQL, HTML, and Prolog are declarative; Python and Java are imperative.
terms.eli16: A coding style where you describe what you want the result to be, not the step-by-step instructions for how to get there.

terms.definition: IBM's chess-playing computer that defeated world champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, becoming the first computer system to beat a reigning world chess champion under standard tournament conditions.
terms.eli16: IBM's chess computer that beat world champion Garry Kasparov in 1997 — a milestone in AI history.

terms.definition: Advanced technology based on substantial scientific or engineering innovation — including AI, quantum computing, biotech, and advanced materials. Typically requires significant R&D and long development timelines.
terms.eli16: Technology based on major scientific breakthroughs — like AI, quantum computing, and biotech — requiring years of R&D.

terms.definition: An AI research laboratory acquired by Google in 2014, known for AlphaGo, AlphaFold, Gemini, and fundamental research in reinforcement learning and AI safety.
terms.eli16: Google's AI research lab, famous for AlphaGo, AlphaFold, and breakthroughs in reinforcement learning and protein folding.

terms.definition: A non-monotonic logic that allows reasoning with defaults — assumptions that hold unless there's specific reason to believe otherwise. Models how humans make reasonable assumptions.
terms.eli16: A form of AI logic that lets you make reasonable default assumptions and revise them when you get contradicting information.

terms.definition: A density-based clustering algorithm that groups together closely packed data points and marks outliers in low-density regions. Unlike k-means, it discovers arbitrary-shaped clusters and doesn't require specifying the number of clusters.
terms.eli16: A clustering algorithm that finds groups of nearby data points automatically, without needing to know how many groups to expect.

terms.definition: A family of knowledge representation formalisms used as the basis for ontology languages like OWL. Provides a formal foundation for describing concepts and their relationships.
terms.eli16: A formal language for describing knowledge and relationships between concepts — the foundation of semantic web ontologies.

terms.definition: A field that models the developmental processes of biological organisms to build robots that learn and adapt over time through interaction with their environment, similar to how children develop.
terms.eli16: Building robots that learn and grow through experience, similar to how children develop skills over time.

terms.definition: A set of practices that combines software development (Dev) and IT operations (Ops) to shorten development cycles, increase deployment frequency, and deliver reliable software through automation and collaboration.
terms.eli16: A way of working where software developers and IT operations teams collaborate closely to ship software faster and more reliably.

terms.definition: An AI system designed to converse with humans through natural language — ranging from simple rule-based chatbots to sophisticated neural systems capable of multi-turn reasoning.
terms.eli16: AI systems designed to have conversations with humans — from simple chatbots to advanced conversational assistants.

terms.definition: An algorithm for finding the shortest paths between nodes in a graph. Widely used in GPS navigation, network routing, and AI pathfinding for non-negative edge weights.
terms.eli16: The classic algorithm for finding the shortest path through a network — used in GPS and network routing.

terms.definition: Cloud-based services that replicate and host IT systems to enable rapid recovery after a disaster. Organizations can failover to cloud replicas and restore operations quickly.
terms.eli16: A cloud service that backs up your entire IT system so you can quickly recover if something catastrophic happens.

terms.definition: AI systems where computation is spread across multiple networked agents or nodes, each with partial information. Enables scalable AI and privacy-preserving approaches like federated learning.
terms.eli16: AI where the intelligence is spread across many computers or agents working together, rather than in one central system.

terms.definition: An open-source platform for building, shipping, and running applications in containers. Docker standardized containerization and became the dominant tool for packaging applications with their dependencies.
terms.eli16: The most popular tool for packaging applications into containers — making software run consistently anywhere.

terms.definition: A type of NoSQL database that stores data as flexible, JSON-like documents rather than rows in tables. Each document can have a different structure, making it ideal for semi-structured data.
terms.eli16: A database that stores data as flexible document files (like JSON) rather than rigid table rows — good for varying data structures.

terms.definition: A framework for programming language models with self-improving prompts. DSPy replaces manual prompt engineering with a declarative API and optimization algorithms that tune prompts automatically.
terms.eli16: A framework that automatically optimizes AI prompts for you — instead of hand-crafting prompts, the system learns the best ones.

terms.definition: A machine learning approach where the model is fully trained before making predictions. The model generalizes from training data upfront. Opposite of lazy learning (like k-NN).
terms.eli16: ML where the model does all its learning upfront during training, before you even ask it any questions.

terms.definition: A proposed test for movie-making AI, analogous to the Turing Test: an AI passes if it can make a film indistinguishable from one made by a human filmmaker. Proposed by critics as an AI creativity benchmark.
terms.eli16: A proposed test for creative AI: can an AI make a movie that's indistinguishable from one made by a human filmmaker?

terms.definition: A type of recurrent neural network with a fixed, randomly initialized reservoir of neurons. Only the output weights are trained, making it computationally efficient for time-series tasks.
terms.eli16: A type of neural network where most connections are fixed and only the output layer learns — fast and good for time-series data.

terms.definition: ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) and ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) are data pipeline patterns for moving data between systems. ELT loads raw data first and transforms in the destination, common with modern cloud data warehouses.
terms.eli16: Data pipeline patterns for moving data between systems: ETL transforms data before loading, ELT loads first then transforms.

terms.definition: An AI agent that has a physical or simulated body and interacts with its environment through sensory perception and physical action. Intelligence arises from the interaction between body and environment.
terms.eli16: An AI with a physical or virtual body that learns by interacting with the world — like a robot that learns by touching and moving.

terms.definition: A theoretical perspective holding that cognitive processes are deeply rooted in the body's interactions with the world. Intelligence is not just in the brain but emerges from body-environment interaction.
terms.eli16: The theory that intelligence isn't just in the brain — it's shaped by having a body and interacting with the physical world.

terms.definition: The phenomenon where complex behaviors or properties arise from simpler components interacting — the whole is more than the sum of its parts. In AI, large models exhibit emergent capabilities not present in smaller versions.
terms.eli16: When complex, surprising abilities arise from combining simple parts — like how individual neurons create human consciousness.

terms.definition: The process of encoding data so that only authorized parties can access it. Uses mathematical algorithms to convert plaintext into ciphertext. Fundamental to cybersecurity and data privacy.
terms.eli16: The process of scrambling data so only authorized people can read it — the basis of secure communication and data privacy.

terms.definition: The deployment of AI technologies within large organizations to automate processes, enhance decision-making, improve customer experience, and generate insights from business data at scale.
terms.eli16: Using AI throughout a large organization to automate work, improve decisions, and gain insights from company data.

terms.definition: A learning paradigm where a model updates its parameters based on the difference between predicted and actual outputs — the error signal drives learning. Backpropagation is error-driven.
terms.eli16: Learning by making mistakes — a model adjusts itself based on how wrong its predictions were.

terms.definition: A software design pattern where components communicate by producing and consuming events. Highly decoupled and scalable — services react to events as they occur rather than polling for changes.
terms.eli16: A software design where different parts of a system communicate by sending and reacting to events, like a notification system.

terms.definition: A risk that could permanently and drastically curtail humanity's long-term potential — including human extinction. Advanced AI is considered a potential existential risk by some researchers.
terms.eli16: A threat that could end or permanently limit humanity's future — advanced AI is one such risk that some researchers take seriously.

terms.definition: In machine learning, a feature is an individual measurable property or characteristic of the data used as input to a model. Features are the variables the model uses to make predictions.
terms.eli16: The individual pieces of information an AI model uses as input — like age, height, or word frequency when making a prediction.

terms.definition: The process of transforming raw data into a set of informative, meaningful features for use in ML models. Can be manual (domain expertise) or automatic (learned by neural networks).
terms.eli16: Pulling out the most informative characteristics from raw data for an AI model to learn from.

terms.definition: The ability of ML models to automatically discover useful representations or features from raw data, rather than requiring manual feature engineering. Deep learning excels at feature learning.
terms.eli16: When an AI learns to identify the most useful patterns in data on its own, without humans specifying what to look for.

terms.definition: The process of selecting a subset of relevant features for use in model construction. Reduces overfitting, improves accuracy, and reduces training time by removing irrelevant or redundant variables.
terms.eli16: Choosing which variables are most useful for an AI model and removing the ones that don't help.

terms.definition: A formal system for representing knowledge using predicates, variables, quantifiers, and logical connectives. More expressive than propositional logic; forms the basis of many AI knowledge representation systems.
terms.eli16: A formal logical language that can express relationships between objects and make general statements about all things — more powerful than simple true/false logic.

terms.definition: An inference strategy that starts from known facts and applies rules to derive new facts until the goal is reached. Used in rule-based expert systems and production systems.
terms.eli16: AI reasoning that starts with known facts and keeps applying rules to derive new conclusions — working toward a goal.

terms.definition: An AI system that has good values and reliably benefits humanity. The term was coined by Eliezer Yudkowsky to describe the goal of ensuring future advanced AI systems are safe and beneficial.
terms.eli16: An AI system with values aligned with human welfare — designed to be reliably helpful and not harmful.

terms.definition: A measure of a model's accuracy on a classification task, combining precision and recall into a single metric. The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
terms.eli16: A single number that combines an AI classifier's precision and recall — a balanced measure of how good it is.

terms.definition: Search functionality that examines all words in every stored document to find matches for a query. More powerful than metadata search — used in search engines, databases, and document management.
terms.eli16: Search that looks through the entire content of documents to find matches, not just titles or tags.

terms.definition: A serverless cloud computing execution model where individual functions are deployed and executed in response to events, with no server management required. AWS Lambda and Google Cloud Functions are examples.
terms.eli16: Serverless computing where you deploy just a single function and it runs automatically when triggered — no server management needed.

terms.definition: An interdisciplinary field that studies possible, probable, and preferable futures to inform decision-making. Uses trend analysis, scenario planning, and forecasting methods.
terms.eli16: The study of possible future scenarios to help organizations and societies plan ahead.

terms.definition: A search technique that finds results that are approximately equal to the search query, tolerating typos, misspellings, and variations. Common in search engines and databases.
terms.eli16: Search that finds results even when they don't exactly match your query — handling typos and variations gracefully.

terms.definition: A set where elements have degrees of membership between 0 and 1, rather than binary membership. Foundation of fuzzy logic, which handles vagueness and partial truth — useful for control systems.
terms.eli16: A mathematical concept where things can partially belong to a category — not just true/false but varying degrees of membership.

terms.definition: The mathematical study of strategic interactions between rational decision-makers. Applications in AI include multi-agent systems, mechanism design, and training GANs.
terms.eli16: The mathematical study of strategic decision-making — how rational players behave when their choices affect each other.

terms.definition: Google's family of lightweight, open-source AI models derived from the same research as Gemini. Available for local deployment, offering strong performance for their size.
terms.eli16: Google's smaller, open-source AI models that can run on your own hardware — derived from the same research as Gemini.

terms.definition: A deep learning architecture consisting of two neural networks — a generator and discriminator — trained in opposition. The generator creates fake data; the discriminator tries to distinguish real from fake. Used for image synthesis, style transfer, and data augmentation.
terms.eli16: Two AI networks competing: one creates fake images, the other tries to spot them — the competition forces both to improve.

terms.definition: The ability of AI systems to play any game given a formal description of the rules, without game-specific programming. Tests general-purpose AI reasoning and planning.
terms.eli16: AI that can learn to play any game just by reading the rules — not pre-programmed for specific games.

terms.definition: A model's ability to perform well on unseen data by learning underlying patterns rather than memorizing training examples. The ultimate goal of supervised learning.
terms.eli16: An AI model's ability to apply what it learned from training examples to new, unseen examples it hasn't seen before.

terms.definition: The difference between a model's training error and its test error — how much worse it performs on unseen data. High generalization error indicates overfitting.
terms.eli16: How much worse an AI model performs on new data compared to its training data — high means it memorized instead of learning.

terms.definition: A model that learns the distribution of training data and can generate new examples from that distribution. Examples include GPT (text), diffusion models (images), and VAEs.
terms.eli16: An AI model that can create new content — text, images, audio — by learning the patterns in existing examples.

terms.definition: OpenAI's architecture for language models that uses the transformer architecture, pre-trained on large text datasets using self-supervised learning. The foundation for ChatGPT and many other AI systems.
terms.eli16: The AI architecture behind ChatGPT — pre-trained on vast amounts of text to understand and generate language.

terms.definition: A search and optimization algorithm inspired by natural selection: a population of candidate solutions evolves through selection, crossover, and mutation over generations.
terms.eli16: An optimization method inspired by evolution — keeping the best solutions, mixing them together, and occasionally adding random changes.

terms.definition: An ensemble learning technique that builds models sequentially, with each new tree correcting residual errors from previous ones using gradient descent. XGBoost and LightGBM are leading implementations.
terms.eli16: A powerful ML technique that builds many decision trees in sequence, each one fixing the mistakes of the previous — widely used in competitions.

terms.definition: A database that uses graph structures (nodes and edges) to store, map, and query relationships between data. Ideal for social networks, recommendation systems, and knowledge graphs.
terms.eli16: A database designed for data with lots of relationships — like social networks — storing connections as first-class citizens.

terms.definition: Neural networks designed to work directly on graph-structured data, learning representations by aggregating information from neighboring nodes. Used in drug discovery, social networks, and knowledge graphs.
terms.eli16: Neural networks that learn from data structured as networks of connected nodes — like social graphs or molecular structures.

terms.definition: An approach to retrieval-augmented generation that uses knowledge graphs to structure and retrieve context for LLMs. Enables more precise reasoning over complex, interconnected information compared to vector-only RAG.
terms.eli16: RAG that uses a knowledge graph to find and connect related information — giving AI more structured context than just text chunks.

terms.definition: The mathematical study of graphs — structures consisting of nodes connected by edges. Foundational for computer science, network analysis, and AI algorithms like pathfinding and clustering.
terms.eli16: The mathematics of networks — studying how nodes and connections behave, underlying algorithms from social network analysis to GPS routing.

terms.definition: A practical problem-solving approach that isn't guaranteed to be optimal but is good enough for most purposes. In AI search, a heuristic estimates the cost to reach a goal, guiding the search.
terms.eli16: A shortcut or rule of thumb that helps solve problems quickly enough — not perfect but good enough for practical use.

terms.definition: In a neural network, layers between the input and output layers that learn intermediate representations. Deep networks have many hidden layers — 'deep' in deep learning refers to this depth.
terms.eli16: The middle layers of a neural network that learn to detect patterns — the 'deep' in deep learning refers to having many of these.

terms.definition: The use of parallel processing and supercomputers to solve complex computational problems much faster than standard computers. Critical for AI training, scientific simulation, and weather forecasting.
terms.eli16: Extremely powerful computing using many processors working together — used for training large AI models and scientific simulations.

terms.definition: An AI system design where human judgment is incorporated into the AI decision-making process — humans review, correct, or approve AI outputs, especially for high-stakes decisions.
terms.eli16: AI systems designed to involve a human reviewer for important decisions — combining AI speed with human judgment.

terms.definition: A computing environment that combines on-premises infrastructure with public and/or private cloud services, with orchestration between them. Allows workloads to move between environments based on needs.
terms.eli16: A mix of your own servers and rented cloud services working together — giving flexibility to run workloads wherever they fit best.

terms.definition: In machine learning, a hyperplane is a decision boundary that separates data into classes. In an n-dimensional feature space, a hyperplane is an (n-1)-dimensional subspace. Support vector machines use hyperplanes.
terms.eli16: A flat boundary (in any number of dimensions) that separates data into different categories — used by support vector machines.

terms.definition: A cloud computing model where virtualized computing infrastructure — servers, storage, networks — is provided on-demand over the internet. AWS EC2, Azure VMs, and Google Compute Engine are examples.
terms.eli16: Renting raw computing infrastructure (servers, storage, networking) from the cloud instead of buying your own hardware.

terms.definition: A computer vision task where an input image is transformed into an output image of a different style, domain, or appearance. Applications include style transfer, colorization, and photo editing with AI.
terms.eli16: AI that transforms one type of image into another — like turning a sketch into a photo or changing a summer scene to winter.

terms.definition: The ability of large language models to learn new tasks from examples provided in the prompt, without updating model weights. A few examples in the prompt guide the model's behavior.
terms.eli16: Teaching an AI new tasks just by showing examples in the prompt — no retraining required, just good examples.

terms.definition: A machine learning approach where models learn from new data continuously, updating incrementally without forgetting previously learned information. Addresses the catastrophic forgetting problem.
terms.eli16: An AI that can keep learning from new data over time without forgetting what it already knew.

terms.definition: The practice of managing and provisioning computing infrastructure through machine-readable configuration files rather than manual processes. Tools: Terraform, Pulumi, AWS CloudFormation.
terms.eli16: Managing your servers and cloud resources using code files instead of manual clicking — making infrastructure reproducible and versioned.

terms.definition: OpenAI's model trained with RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) to follow instructions better than base GPT-3. The precursor to ChatGPT — demonstrated that RLHF dramatically improves helpfulness.
terms.eli16: OpenAI's model trained to follow instructions well — the stepping stone to ChatGPT, showing that human feedback improves AI helpfulness.

terms.definition: Fine-tuning a pre-trained language model on datasets of instruction-response pairs to make it better at following user instructions. A key technique in making LLMs practically useful.
terms.eli16: Training an AI model on examples of instructions and good responses so it learns to follow directions reliably.

terms.definition: The use of technology to enhance human intellectual capabilities — helping people think, remember, and reason better. Often contrasted with full AI replacement.
terms.eli16: Using technology to make humans smarter and more capable — extending human intelligence rather than replacing it.

terms.definition: A hypothetical scenario where an AI system improves its own intelligence, enabling it to make further improvements in a rapid recursive cycle, quickly surpassing human intelligence.
terms.eli16: The hypothetical scenario where an AI improves itself, enabling faster self-improvement in a runaway cycle toward superintelligence.

terms.definition: An autonomous entity that perceives its environment through sensors, processes information, and acts on the environment through actuators to achieve its goals.
terms.eli16: An autonomous system that senses its environment, thinks, and takes actions to achieve a goal — the core concept of AI agents.

terms.definition: Control systems that use AI techniques — neural networks, fuzzy logic, expert systems — to control complex dynamic systems that are difficult to model mathematically.
terms.eli16: Control systems that use AI techniques to manage complex machines or processes that are too complicated for traditional formulas.

terms.definition: Combining RPA (Robotic Process Automation) with AI capabilities like NLP and ML to automate complex, judgment-intensive processes that go beyond simple rule-based tasks.
terms.eli16: Automation that handles complex tasks requiring judgment — combining robots that follow rules with AI that can understand context.

terms.definition: In AI and ML, the process of understanding why and how a model makes predictions — making black-box models more transparent. Related to explainability and transparency.
terms.eli16: Understanding why an AI model made a particular decision — making its reasoning visible and understandable.

terms.definition: In RL and AI, intrinsic motivation refers to reward signals generated internally by the agent — like curiosity or novelty — rather than from external rewards. Helps exploration in sparse-reward environments.
terms.eli16: When an AI explores and learns driven by internal curiosity rather than external rewards — helping it discover things even without explicit feedback.

terms.definition: A structured diagram that breaks down a complex problem into its component parts in a hierarchical, MECE (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive) way. Used in consulting and AI reasoning.
terms.eli16: A diagram that breaks a big problem into smaller sub-problems in a tree structure — used to organize complex thinking.

terms.definition: An open-source service mesh that provides traffic management, security, and observability for microservices running on Kubernetes. Manages communication between services without changing application code.
terms.eli16: A system for managing how microservices talk to each other — handling traffic, security, and monitoring automatically.

terms.definition: An algorithm for performing exact inference in probabilistic graphical models (Bayesian networks and Markov networks) by converting the graph into a tree structure.
terms.eli16: An algorithm for calculating probabilities in complex networks of related random variables.

terms.definition: A class of algorithms that use kernel functions to transform data into higher-dimensional spaces where linear separation becomes possible. Support Vector Machines are the most prominent kernel method.
terms.eli16: A math trick that transforms data into a higher-dimensional space where patterns that weren't separable become separable.

terms.definition: A simple supervised learning algorithm that classifies data points based on the majority label of their k nearest neighbors in feature space. Also used for regression.
terms.eli16: A simple ML algorithm that classifies something by looking at what its closest neighbors are labeled — majority vote wins.

terms.definition: The process of extracting knowledge from experts or data and representing it in a form usable by AI systems. A bottleneck in building expert systems — known as the 'knowledge acquisition bottleneck'.
terms.eli16: The process of capturing knowledge from human experts or data to build AI knowledge bases — historically one of AI's hardest challenges.

terms.definition: An AI system that uses a knowledge base of domain-specific facts and rules to reason and solve problems. The basis of expert systems in medicine, engineering, and law.
terms.eli16: An AI system that uses a database of expert knowledge and rules to answer questions and solve problems in a specific domain.

terms.definition: A technique for training a smaller 'student' model to mimic a larger 'teacher' model. The student learns from the teacher's soft probability outputs, compressing knowledge into a more efficient model.
terms.eli16: Compressing a large AI model into a smaller one by training the small model to imitate the large one's outputs.

terms.definition: Automatically extracting structured information from unstructured or semi-structured sources (text, web pages, databases) to populate knowledge bases.
terms.eli16: Automatically pulling structured facts and relationships from unstructured text or other sources.

terms.definition: An unsupervised learning algorithm that partitions data into k clusters by iteratively assigning points to the nearest centroid and updating centroids. Simple but widely used for data segmentation.
terms.eli16: A clustering algorithm that groups data into k clusters by finding the natural center of each group.

terms.definition: An open-source ML platform built on Kubernetes for deploying, scaling, and managing ML workflows in production. Provides pipelines, model serving, and experiment tracking.
terms.eli16: A platform for running machine learning workflows on Kubernetes — managing training, deployment, and monitoring of ML models.

terms.definition: An open-source container orchestration system for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. Originally developed by Google, now the industry standard.
terms.eli16: The industry-standard system for automatically managing containers across many servers — handling deployment, scaling, and recovery.

terms.definition: Google's conversational language model trained specifically for open-ended dialogue. Known for a 2022 incident where an engineer claimed it was sentient. Later evolved into Bard and Gemini.
terms.eli16: Google's conversational AI model that became famous when a Google engineer claimed it was sentient — it later evolved into Bard and Gemini.

terms.definition: A framework for building applications with large language models, providing abstractions for chaining LLM calls, integrating tools, managing memory, and building agents.
terms.eli16: A popular toolkit for building AI applications that chain together multiple LLM calls, tools, and memory components.

terms.definition: A statistical model that assigns probabilities to sequences of words, used for text generation, speech recognition, and translation. Modern LLMs like GPT are large-scale neural language models.
terms.eli16: An AI model that learns the patterns of language — predicting likely next words — forming the foundation of modern AI writing and conversation.

terms.definition: A machine learning approach that defers processing until prediction time, storing all training examples. K-nearest neighbors is the classic example — generalizes locally at query time.
terms.eli16: ML that doesn't build a model upfront — instead it stores all training data and figures things out at prediction time.

terms.definition: The process of updating or replacing outdated IT systems with modern technologies while preserving business functionality. AI is increasingly used to accelerate code migration and documentation.
terms.eli16: Upgrading old, outdated software systems to modern technology while keeping the business running.

terms.definition: The process of reducing a word to its base or dictionary form (lemma). 'Running' → 'run', 'better' → 'good'. Used in NLP for text normalization.
terms.eli16: Reducing words to their base form in NLP — so 'running', 'ran', and 'runs' all become 'run' for analysis.

terms.definition: One of the oldest high-level programming languages (1958), historically important in AI research. Known for its symbolic computation capabilities, code-as-data philosophy, and use in early AI systems.
terms.eli16: One of the oldest programming languages, historically the language of AI research — famous for treating code and data the same way.

terms.definition: MLOps: practices for deploying and maintaining ML models in production. LLMOps: the same for large language models, including prompt management, fine-tuning pipelines, and evaluation frameworks.
terms.eli16: The operational practices for running AI models reliably in production — monitoring, updating, and managing them at scale.

terms.definition: Distributing network traffic or computational workloads across multiple servers or resources to prevent overload and ensure availability. Critical for scalable AI inference serving.
terms.eli16: Spreading incoming requests across multiple servers so no single server gets overwhelmed — keeping systems fast and available.

terms.definition: A programming paradigm based on formal logic. Programs are expressed as logical facts and rules; a query engine infers answers. Prolog is the most prominent logic programming language.
terms.eli16: A programming style based on logic — you state facts and rules, and the computer figures out the answers automatically.

terms.definition: Development platforms that allow creating applications through visual interfaces and pre-built components with minimal or no hand-coding. AI is increasingly a key feature of these platforms.
terms.eli16: Platforms that let non-programmers build apps through drag-and-drop interfaces and visual tools — little to no coding required.

terms.definition: Systematic errors in AI predictions caused by prejudiced or unrepresentative training data, flawed model design, or biased deployment. Can perpetuate or amplify societal biases.
terms.eli16: When an AI system produces unfair or discriminatory results because its training data or design contained human biases.

terms.definition: The ability of AI systems to analyze and understand audio signals — including music, speech, environmental sounds, and acoustic events.
terms.eli16: AI that can understand and analyze sounds — music, speech, or environmental noises.

terms.definition: The ability of AI systems to interpret sensory input from the physical world — vision, audio, touch, etc. — enabling machines to understand their environment.
terms.eli16: An AI's ability to sense and interpret the physical world through cameras, microphones, and other sensors.

terms.definition: Automated translation of text or speech from one language to another using AI. Modern neural machine translation (NMT) uses transformer models and achieves near-human quality for many language pairs.
terms.eli16: AI that automatically translates text between languages — like Google Translate or DeepL.

terms.definition: The ability of AI systems to interpret and understand visual information from the world — images and video. Applications: object detection, facial recognition, medical imaging.
terms.eli16: AI that can see and understand images and video — recognizing objects, people, and scenes.

terms.definition: A stochastic model describing a sequence of possible events where the probability of each event depends only on the state of the previous event (Markov property). Foundation for many AI and ML algorithms.
terms.eli16: A probability model where the next state depends only on the current state — the basis for many AI prediction systems.

terms.definition: The selection of the best element from a set of available alternatives according to a criterion. In ML, optimization algorithms like gradient descent minimize the loss function during training.
terms.eli16: The mathematical process of finding the best solution — minimizing errors or maximizing performance — central to all ML training.

terms.definition: A field of economics and AI concerned with designing rules for strategic interactions to achieve desired outcomes. Used in auction design, resource allocation, and multi-agent AI systems.
terms.eli16: Designing the rules of a game so that rational players' self-interested behavior leads to good outcomes — used in auctions and AI systems.

terms.definition: An interdisciplinary field combining mechanical engineering, electronics, computer science, and AI to design intelligent machines and robotic systems.
terms.eli16: The engineering field that combines mechanical, electronic, and AI systems — used to build robots and smart machines.

terms.definition: A higher-level procedure or framework for finding good solutions to optimization problems by combining heuristics. Examples: simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization.
terms.eli16: A general problem-solving strategy that combines simpler heuristics to find good solutions to hard optimization problems.

terms.definition: An architectural style that structures applications as a collection of small, independently deployable services, each running in its own process and communicating via APIs.
terms.eli16: Building apps as many small, independent services that each do one thing — more flexible and scalable than one big monolithic app.

terms.definition: An AI art generation service that creates images from text descriptions, known for its distinctive aesthetic quality. Operates primarily through Discord and has become one of the leading image generation platforms.
terms.eli16: A popular AI image generator known for beautiful, artistic images — you describe an image and it creates it.

terms.definition: A formal verification technique that exhaustively and automatically checks whether a system satisfies a given specification. Used to verify software, hardware, and AI system safety properties.
terms.eli16: Automatically verifying that a system or AI behaves correctly according to a formal specification — catching bugs through exhaustive checking.

terms.definition: Anthropic's open standard protocol that allows AI models to connect with external data sources, tools, and services in a standardized way. Enables AI applications to access real-time information and perform actions.
terms.eli16: Anthropic's open standard for connecting AI models to external tools and data — making it easy to give AI access to any service.

terms.definition: MongoDB is a leading NoSQL document database storing data as flexible JSON-like documents. NoSQL broadly refers to non-relational databases optimized for scalability, flexibility, and specific data models.
terms.eli16: MongoDB is a popular database that stores data as flexible JSON documents instead of rigid tables — great for rapidly changing data structures.

terms.definition: A heuristic search algorithm that uses random sampling to evaluate positions in a game tree. Used in AlphaGo and many game-playing AI systems to handle games with enormous search spaces.
terms.eli16: A search algorithm that explores game possibilities by running random simulations — a key technique in AI game playing.

terms.definition: A strategy of using services from multiple cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP) simultaneously, avoiding vendor lock-in and optimizing for best-of-breed services.
terms.eli16: Using multiple cloud providers at once — picking the best services from Amazon, Google, and Microsoft rather than committing to just one.

terms.definition: A feedforward neural network with one or more hidden layers between input and output. The classic neural network architecture, trained with backpropagation.
terms.eli16: The classic neural network: layers of artificial neurons connected together, learning by adjusting connection weights.

terms.definition: An early expert system developed at Stanford in the 1970s to diagnose bacterial infections and recommend antibiotics. One of the most successful early AI medical systems, demonstrating expert-system feasibility.
terms.eli16: One of the first successful AI medical systems from the 1970s — diagnosed bacterial infections better than many doctors.

terms.definition: A probabilistic classifier based on Bayes' theorem with the 'naive' assumption that features are independent. Fast, interpretable, and works well for text classification and spam filtering.
terms.eli16: A simple but effective AI classifier that uses probability and assumes all features are independent — great for spam filtering.

terms.definition: An NLP task that identifies and classifies named entities in text — people, organizations, locations, dates — into predefined categories.
terms.eli16: AI that reads text and identifies important entities — like finding all the names, places, and organizations mentioned.

terms.definition: Programming using natural language instructions rather than formal programming syntax. AI coding assistants and systems like GitHub Copilot enable natural language to code translation.
terms.eli16: Programming by writing instructions in plain English instead of formal code — AI translates your words into working software.

terms.definition: Machine translation that uses neural networks (particularly transformers) to translate text. Replaced statistical MT as the dominant approach, enabling near-human quality translation.
terms.eli16: AI translation using neural networks — the technology behind Google Translate's modern, natural-sounding translations.

terms.definition: A neural network architecture augmented with an external memory matrix and read/write attention mechanisms, giving it capabilities similar to a Turing machine — a differentiable computer.
terms.eli16: A neural network that can read from and write to external memory, making it capable of algorithms that regular neural networks can't do.

terms.definition: An algorithm that can exhibit different behaviors on different runs for the same input, either due to random choices or parallel exploration. Many AI search algorithms are nondeterministic.
terms.eli16: An algorithm that might give different results each time it runs, often using randomness to explore solutions.

terms.definition: NP is the class of problems verifiable in polynomial time. NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP; NP-hard problems are at least as hard. The P vs NP question (whether P=NP) is unsolved.
terms.eli16: A classification of hard computational problems — NP-complete problems have no known fast solution but answers can be quickly verified.

terms.definition: A data storage architecture that manages data as objects (data + metadata + unique ID) rather than files or blocks. Infinitely scalable and ideal for unstructured data. AWS S3 is the dominant example.
terms.eli16: Cloud storage that treats everything as an object with a unique ID — infinitely scalable storage for files, images, and backups.

terms.definition: The principle that among competing hypotheses, the one with the fewest assumptions should be selected. In ML, relates to model simplicity: simpler models are preferred over complex ones when both explain the data equally well.
terms.eli16: The principle that the simplest explanation is usually correct — in AI, prefer simpler models when they work as well as complex ones.

terms.definition: A machine learning approach where the model is trained on the complete dataset all at once, then deployed. The model doesn't update when new data arrives — opposite of online learning.
terms.eli16: ML where the model trains on all data at once and then stays fixed — no updating after deployment.

terms.definition: A machine learning approach where the model updates incrementally as each new data example arrives, rather than retraining on the full dataset. Used when data arrives in streams.
terms.eli16: ML where the model updates itself continuously as new data comes in — learning in real time.
