terms.definition: An open-source, high-performance key-value store forked from Redis after licensing changes. Maintained by the Linux Foundation with backing from AWS, Google, and others as a Redis alternative.
terms.eli16: An open-source Redis alternative maintained by the Linux Foundation — emerged after Redis changed its licensing.

terms.definition: Google's video generation model capable of creating high-quality, realistic videos from text and image prompts. Integrated into YouTube and Google products.
terms.eli16: Google's AI video generator — creates high-quality, realistic videos from text descriptions, integrated into YouTube's creative tools.

terms.definition: Google Cloud's managed search service that uses AI to enable semantic and structured search across enterprise data. Combines vector search, keyword search, and generative AI answers.
terms.eli16: Google Cloud's AI-powered enterprise search — understanding the meaning of queries to find relevant information across your company's data.

terms.definition: A technology that hosts desktop operating systems on centralized servers in a data center. Users access their desktops remotely from any device — AI is used to optimize performance and security.
terms.eli16: Technology that runs your desktop computer in the cloud — access your full desktop environment from any device anywhere.

terms.definition: DeepMind's deep neural network model for generating raw audio waveforms. Originally created for text-to-speech, it produces extremely natural-sounding speech and is integrated into Google Assistant.
terms.eli16: DeepMind's AI model for generating natural-sounding audio — the technology behind some of Google Assistant's most realistic voices.

terms.definition: OpenAI's automatic speech recognition model trained on 680,000 hours of multilingual audio. Highly accurate, supports 99+ languages, and is open-source — widely used for transcription.
terms.eli16: OpenAI's speech recognition AI trained on massive amounts of audio — one of the most accurate free transcription tools available.

terms.definition: A technique for learning word vector representations from large text corpora. Words used in similar contexts get similar vectors, enabling mathematical operations on word meanings.
terms.eli16: A method for representing words as numbers (vectors) so that words with similar meanings have similar numbers — enabling math on language.

terms.definition: A security model based on the principle 'never trust, always verify' — requiring continuous authentication and authorization for every user and device, even inside the network perimeter.
terms.eli16: A security approach that never assumes anyone is trustworthy by default — everyone must continuously prove who they are and why they need access.

terms.definition: A form of logic programming that extends standard logic with abduction — hypothesizing new facts to explain observations. Used in AI for diagnosis, planning, and natural language understanding.
terms.eli16: AI reasoning that works backwards from observations to figure out the most likely explanation.

terms.definition: A neural network based on Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy inference, combining neural networks' learning ability with fuzzy logic's interpretability. Used for control and pattern recognition.
terms.eli16: A hybrid AI combining fuzzy logic and neural networks — human-like reasoning with machine learning.

terms.definition: AI systems that autonomously plan and execute multi-step tasks using tools, browsing, code execution, and APIs to achieve goals — not just answering single questions.
terms.eli16: AI that actually does things — browsing the web, writing code, and completing multi-step tasks on your behalf.

terms.definition: Amazon's managed platform for building generative AI applications using foundation models from Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, and others without managing infrastructure.
terms.eli16: Amazon's cloud service for building AI apps using leading AI models, without managing servers.

terms.definition: Smart environments where embedded sensors, AI, and systems adapt seamlessly to human presence. Technology is woven invisibly into surroundings.
terms.eli16: Technology built invisibly into your environment that automatically senses and responds to your needs.

terms.definition: A declarative programming paradigm for difficult search problems. Programs are logical rules; the system finds stable models satisfying all rules simultaneously.
terms.eli16: A programming style where you describe rules and the computer automatically finds all valid solutions.

terms.definition: A probabilistic optimization technique inspired by ant pheromone behavior. Applied to routing, scheduling, and combinatorial optimization problems.
terms.eli16: An optimization algorithm inspired by how ants find the shortest path to food — applied to routing and scheduling.

terms.main_term: approximate string matching / fuzzy string searching
terms.definition: Techniques for finding strings approximately matching a pattern, tolerating typos and variations. Used in spell-checkers, search engines, and bioinformatics.
terms.eli16: Searching for text even with typos or slight differences — finding close matches, not just exact ones.

terms.definition: A computational intelligence system inspired by the vertebrate immune system. Used for anomaly detection, fault tolerance, and optimization by mimicking immune response.
terms.eli16: An AI system inspired by the human immune system — it learns to recognize and respond to unusual patterns.

terms.definition: An XML-based markup language for creating conversational AI chatbots, originally developed for ALICE chatbot. Defines pattern-matching rules for dialogue.
terms.eli16: A language for programming chatbots by defining patterns and responses — used by early chatbot systems like ALICE.

terms.definition: A computing system modeled loosely on biological neural networks, consisting of interconnected nodes organized in layers that learn patterns through weighted connections.
terms.eli16: A computer system inspired by the human brain, made of connected artificial neurons that learn from examples.

terms.definition: A hypothetical AI that surpasses human intelligence across all domains — not just specific tasks but general reasoning, creativity, and problem-solving.
terms.eli16: A hypothetical future AI smarter than any human in every possible way.

terms.definition: A logic-based AI knowledge representation framework that models attributional knowledge — properties, relationships, and exceptions. Part of the MIST (Most Informative Sentences in Text) research.
terms.eli16: A formal system for representing knowledge about properties and relationships between concepts in AI.

terms.definition: Technology that overlays digital information — images, text, 3D objects — onto the real world through a phone or headset. Used in gaming, navigation, and industry.
terms.eli16: Digital visuals and information overlaid on the real world through your phone or special glasses.

terms.definition: Computing where systems manage themselves — self-configuring, self-healing, self-optimizing, and self-protecting — inspired by the human autonomic nervous system.
terms.eli16: Computing systems that manage themselves automatically without human intervention — fixing problems and optimizing performance.

terms.definition: An extension of backpropagation for training recursive neural networks on structured data like trees and graphs, propagating gradients through the graph structure.
terms.eli16: A training algorithm for neural networks that process tree or graph-structured data.

terms.definition: An algorithm for training recurrent neural networks by unrolling the network through time steps and computing gradients across the full sequence.
terms.eli16: The algorithm that trains RNNs by unfolding the network over time and learning how past steps contributed to errors.

terms.definition: A population-based metaheuristic optimization algorithm inspired by the food foraging behavior of honey bees. Scout bees explore the search space; recruited bees exploit promising areas.
terms.eli16: An optimization algorithm inspired by how bees scout for flowers and recruit others to the best ones.

terms.definition: An interdisciplinary field studying behaviors, behavioral patterns, and behavioral intelligence using computational methods, data mining, and AI.
terms.eli16: The study of behavioral patterns using AI and data science — understanding how people, animals, or systems behave.

terms.definition: A modular, hierarchical control structure used in game AI and robotics to organize complex behaviors. More maintainable than finite state machines for complex agents.
terms.eli16: A tree-shaped blueprint for organizing an AI character's or robot's decisions and behaviors.

terms.definition: An AI agent architecture where agents act based on their beliefs (world model), desires (goals), and intentions (committed plans). Popular in multi-agent systems.
terms.eli16: An AI agent model based on beliefs (what it knows), desires (what it wants), and intentions (what it's committed to doing).

terms.definition: Cloud storage designed for unstructured binary data — images, videos, documents. Scalable object storage like AWS S3 and Azure Blob Storage.
terms.eli16: Cloud storage for large files like images, videos, and backups — storing raw binary data at any scale.

terms.definition: The problem of determining if there's an assignment of truth values making a Boolean formula true. The first NP-complete problem; SAT solvers are key AI tools.
terms.eli16: The classic hard problem of finding truth/false assignments that satisfy a logical formula — fundamental to computer science.

terms.definition: An ensemble technique training multiple models on different random data subsets, then combining their predictions. Reduces variance and prevents overfitting.
terms.eli16: An ML technique training many models on different random samples and averaging their predictions for better accuracy.

terms.definition: Technologies that interface directly with the brain — brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), neural implants, and neurofeedback systems — enabling direct communication between brains and machines.
terms.eli16: Technology that connects computers directly to the brain — from medical neural implants to Neuralink-style brain-computer interfaces.

terms.definition: Technologies and processes that transform raw data into actionable insights for business decision-making through dashboards, reporting, and data visualization.
terms.eli16: Tools that turn company data into charts and insights to help leaders make better decisions.

terms.definition: A neural network architecture using groups of neurons (capsules) representing entities and properties, better handling spatial relationships than standard CNNs.
terms.eli16: A neural network where groups of neurons represent objects and their spatial properties — designed to better understand 3D structure.

terms.definition: An AI problem-solving approach that retrieves and adapts solutions from similar past cases. Used in expert systems and recommendation engines.
terms.eli16: AI that solves new problems by finding similar past situations and adapting their solutions.

terms.definition: Organizing items into hierarchical groups based on shared characteristics. Category trees provide hierarchical organization of concepts used in knowledge management.
terms.eli16: Organizing things into hierarchical groups based on shared properties — like a tree of categories and subcategories.

terms.definition: A database technique that tracks all changes (inserts, updates, deletes) in real time, enabling downstream systems to react to data changes immediately.
terms.eli16: Technology that watches a database for any changes and immediately notifies other systems — a live feed of all data updates.

terms.definition: OpenAI's model that learns visual concepts from natural language by training on image-text pairs. Enables zero-shot image classification and powers many image generation models.
terms.eli16: OpenAI's model that understands both images and text together — trained by matching millions of images to their descriptions.

terms.definition: Unsupervised ML technique grouping similar data points without predefined labels. Used in customer segmentation, anomaly detection, and exploration.
terms.eli16: AI that automatically groups similar data points together without being told what the groups should be.

terms.definition: An incremental concept formation system that organizes observations into a concept hierarchy by maximizing category utility. One of the earliest unsupervised learning algorithms.
terms.eli16: An early AI clustering algorithm that builds a hierarchy of concepts by grouping observations with maximum utility.

terms.definition: A machine learning system that combines predictions from multiple models (committee members) to produce more accurate or robust results than any individual model.
terms.eli16: An ensemble approach using multiple AI models that vote together — the combined judgment is more reliable than any one model alone.

terms.definition: The use of computers and algorithms to simulate molecular systems, predict chemical properties, and model reactions. AI has transformed drug discovery and materials science through computational chemistry.
terms.eli16: Using computers to simulate molecules and predict how chemicals behave — AI is revolutionizing drug discovery this way.

terms.definition: An interdisciplinary field combining cybernetics (study of control and communication in animals and machines) with computational methods and AI.
terms.eli16: The computational study of how control and communication work in living beings and machines.

terms.definition: The study and development of AI systems that understand, generate, and respond to humor — including joke generation, pun detection, and humor appreciation.
terms.eli16: Teaching computers to understand and generate jokes — a surprisingly hard AI problem.

terms.definition: A set of biologically inspired AI methods including neural networks, fuzzy systems, and evolutionary algorithms. Differs from classical AI by using adaptive, data-driven approaches.
terms.eli16: AI methods inspired by nature — neural networks, fuzzy logic, and evolutionary algorithms — that learn and adapt from data.

terms.definition: The mathematical study of machine learning algorithms — analyzing sample complexity, computational complexity, and the learnability of different concept classes.
terms.eli16: The mathematics of machine learning — rigorously studying when and how algorithms can learn from data.

terms.definition: Mathematics focused on developing algorithms and methods for solving mathematical problems using computers — including numerical analysis, optimization, and simulation.
terms.eli16: Mathematical methods designed to be computed by machines — algorithms for numerical calculations and problem-solving.

terms.definition: The application of computational methods to solve problems in number theory. Fundamental to cryptography, particularly RSA and elliptic curve cryptography.
terms.eli16: Using computers to solve problems in number theory — the foundation of modern encryption and cybersecurity.

terms.definition: A formal specification of a problem that a computer algorithm must solve — defined by the relationship between input instances and valid outputs.
terms.eli16: A precisely defined problem that can be solved by a computer algorithm — the building blocks of computer science.

terms.definition: The intersection of statistics and computer science, using algorithms and computational methods to analyze data when traditional formulas are impractical.
terms.eli16: Statistical analysis using computer algorithms instead of manual formulas — essential for handling modern large datasets.

terms.definition: The use of computers to automatically generate, evaluate, and optimize designs — from circuit layouts to mechanical components — using AI and optimization algorithms.
terms.eli16: Using AI to automatically generate and optimize designs — from circuit boards to mechanical parts.

terms.definition: A heuristic that satisfies the triangle inequality — the estimated cost from node n is never greater than the edge cost plus the estimated cost from the successor. Stronger than admissibility.
terms.eli16: A search heuristic that never gives a higher estimate to a node than the actual cost through its neighbors — ensures A* never re-explores nodes.

terms.definition: A machine learning framework that expresses learning and inference as constrained optimization over conditional (probabilistic) models. Integrates domain knowledge as constraints.
terms.eli16: An ML framework that incorporates domain rules as constraints during both learning and prediction.

terms.definition: A form of logic programming that extends it with constraints over domains. Used for scheduling, planning, and combinatorial problems where variables must satisfy relationships.
terms.eli16: A programming approach combining logic programming with constraint solving — powerful for scheduling and optimization problems.

terms.definition: In genetic algorithms, the process of combining parts of two parent solutions to create offspring solutions. Analogous to biological reproduction and chromosome recombination.
terms.eli16: In genetic algorithms, mixing parts of two solutions together to create new ones — like biological reproduction.

terms.definition: The process of collecting and loading data from various sources into a storage or processing system. Can be batch (periodic) or streaming (continuous).
terms.eli16: The process of collecting and loading data from various sources into a system where it can be analyzed.

terms.definition: A declarative logic programming language used as a query and rule language for deductive databases. More restricted than Prolog but always terminates. Used in program analysis and knowledge bases.
terms.eli16: A simple logic programming language for querying databases using rules — always terminates, unlike general logic programming.

terms.definition: An information system supporting business decision-making by combining data analysis, models, and visualization to help analyze complex situations.
terms.eli16: Software that helps leaders make better decisions by organizing relevant information and presenting useful analyses.

terms.definition: The study of how rational agents make choices under uncertainty, combining probability theory and utility theory. Foundation for AI planning, reinforcement learning, and game theory.
terms.eli16: The mathematical study of how to make optimal decisions when outcomes are uncertain.

terms.definition: Neural network layers that perform the reverse operation of convolution — upsampling feature maps. Used in image segmentation, generative models, and visualizing CNN features.
terms.eli16: Neural network layers that reverse convolution — scaling images up rather than down, used in image generation and segmentation.

terms.definition: An AI system that classifies new instances by deducing their category from a knowledge base of logical rules and facts, rather than learning from statistical patterns.
terms.eli16: An AI classifier that uses logical rules to deduce what category something belongs to — reasoning rather than pattern matching.

terms.definition: A family of knowledge representation formalisms forming the basis for ontology languages like OWL. Provides formal foundation for describing concepts and their relationships.
terms.eli16: A formal language for representing knowledge about concepts and their relationships — the foundation of semantic web ontologies.

terms.definition: In AI, the process of identifying faults, diseases, or problems from observed symptoms using reasoning systems, expert knowledge, or ML models. A classic application of expert systems.
terms.eli16: AI identifying what's wrong with a system or patient based on observed symptoms — from medical diagnosis to fault detection.

terms.definition: Generative AI models that learn to create data by reversing a gradual noising process. State-of-the-art for image generation (Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 3, Midjourney).
terms.eli16: AI image generators that start from random noise and gradually 'denoise' it into a coherent image — the technology behind Stable Diffusion.

terms.definition: A system where state changes occur at distinct, countable points in time rather than continuously. Used in modeling digital computers, manufacturing processes, and AI simulations.
terms.eli16: A system that changes in discrete steps rather than continuously — like a board game where pieces move one at a time.

terms.definition: Cloud-based services that replicate IT systems to enable rapid recovery after disasters. Organizations fail over to cloud replicas and restore operations quickly.
terms.eli16: Cloud backup services that let you restore your entire IT system quickly if a disaster destroys your infrastructure.

terms.definition: AI systems where computation is distributed across multiple networked agents, each with partial information. Enables scalable, privacy-preserving approaches like federated learning.
terms.eli16: AI spread across many computers or agents working together, rather than centralized in one system.

terms.definition: A logical framework for reasoning about knowledge and how it changes as agents exchange information or observe events. Used in multi-agent AI and game theory.
terms.eli16: A formal logic for reasoning about what agents know and how their knowledge changes when they share information.

terms.definition: A recurrent neural network with a fixed random reservoir of neurons. Only output weights are trained, making it computationally efficient for time-series and sequence tasks.
terms.eli16: A type of neural network where most connections are random and fixed — only the output learns, making training very fast.

terms.definition: Running AI models on edge devices (phones, sensors, IoT) rather than in the cloud. Reduces latency, improves privacy, and enables offline operation.
terms.eli16: AI running directly on your device rather than in the cloud — faster, more private, and works without internet.

terms.definition: An AI with a physical or simulated body that interacts with its environment through sensory perception and physical action. Intelligence emerges from body-environment interaction.
terms.eli16: An AI with a body — physical or virtual — that learns by interacting with the world rather than just processing text.

terms.definition: Complex behaviors or capabilities arising from simpler components interacting — the whole exceeds the sum of parts. In AI, large models exhibit emergent capabilities absent in smaller versions.
terms.eli16: When surprising new abilities appear in AI systems as they scale up — capabilities that weren't present in smaller versions.

terms.definition: Optimization algorithms inspired by biological evolution: populations of solutions undergo selection, crossover, and mutation to improve over generations.
terms.eli16: Optimization methods that mimic evolution — keeping best solutions, mixing them, and occasionally mutating them.

terms.definition: A family of algorithms inspired by biological evolution for optimization and search. Encompasses genetic algorithms, evolutionary programming, and genetic programming.
terms.eli16: The broader field of AI algorithms inspired by biological evolution — genetic algorithms are the most common type.

terms.definition: A machine learning approach where the classifier's structure and parameters are continuously updated as new training data arrives, adapting to concept drift.
terms.eli16: A classifier that continuously evolves and updates itself as new data arrives — adapting to changes over time.

terms.definition: Simple decision tree heuristics with one exit branch at each node, designed for quick decisions with limited information. Based on Gigerenzer's research on heuristic decision-making.
terms.eli16: Extremely simple decision trees designed for fast, good-enough decisions with minimal information — inspired by how humans actually make decisions.

terms.definition: The ability of ML models to automatically discover useful features from raw data. Deep learning excels at learning hierarchical representations without manual feature engineering.
terms.eli16: When AI automatically learns what features to look for in data, rather than being told explicitly what matters.

terms.definition: In knowledge representation (especially situation calculus), a fluent is a property of the world that can change over time due to actions. Used in AI planning and reasoning about change.
terms.eli16: A property in AI logic that can change over time — like 'the door is open' — used in planning systems.

terms.definition: A language defined by precise mathematical rules — its syntax is completely specified by a formal grammar. Programming languages and logic languages are formal languages.
terms.eli16: A precisely defined language with exact mathematical rules — programming languages are formal languages, unlike natural spoken languages.

terms.definition: In AI, a data structure representing a stereotyped situation, containing slots for attributes and values. Frames enable knowledge representation with defaults and inheritance.
terms.eli16: A data structure in AI that represents a typical situation with slots for its properties — like a template for 'restaurant' or 'airplane'.

terms.definition: A knowledge representation language based on frames — structured objects with slots representing properties, values, and relationships between concepts.
terms.eli16: A language for building AI knowledge bases using frame structures — templates for real-world concepts with their typical properties.

terms.definition: The challenge in AI of representing and reasoning about what does NOT change when an action is performed. A fundamental problem in knowledge representation and planning.
terms.eli16: A classic AI challenge: when an action happens, how does an AI know what stayed the same? Specifying non-change is harder than it sounds.

terms.definition: Serverless cloud computing where individual functions execute in response to events. No server management — AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions are examples.
terms.eli16: Serverless computing where you deploy just a single function that runs when triggered — no server management needed.

terms.definition: A control system based on fuzzy logic that handles imprecise inputs and produces control outputs using linguistic rules like 'if temperature is high, then cooling is strong'.
terms.eli16: A control system that uses fuzzy logic rules instead of precise math — letting you express control logic in natural language.

terms.definition: A deep learning architecture with two competing networks — a generator creating fake data and a discriminator distinguishing real from fake. Used for image synthesis and style transfer.
terms.eli16: Two neural networks competing: one generates fake images, the other detects them — the competition makes both improve.

terms.definition: The ability of AI systems to play any game described by formal rules, without game-specific programming. Tests general-purpose AI reasoning and planning.
terms.eli16: AI that can learn to play any game just by reading the rules — not programmed specifically for any single game.

terms.definition: OpenAI's transformer-based language model architecture pre-trained on large text datasets. The foundation for ChatGPT and many other AI systems.
terms.eli16: The AI architecture behind ChatGPT — pre-trained on vast text to understand and generate language.

terms.definition: A search and optimization algorithm inspired by natural selection: populations of solutions evolve through selection, crossover, and mutation.
terms.eli16: An optimization method inspired by evolution — keeping the best solutions, mixing them together, and adding random mutations.

terms.definition: Operations applied to solutions in genetic algorithms — primarily selection (choosing parents), crossover (combining parents), and mutation (random changes).
terms.eli16: The three operations in genetic algorithms: selecting good solutions, combining them, and randomly tweaking them.

terms.definition: A swarm intelligence optimization algorithm inspired by glowworms that use luminescence to attract mates. Agents exchange luminescence signals to find optimal positions.
terms.eli16: An optimization algorithm inspired by glowworms attracting each other with light — agents share signals to find the best solutions.

terms.definition: A data structure consisting of nodes (vertices) connected by edges. Can be directed (edges have direction) or undirected. Foundation for network analysis, pathfinding, and knowledge graphs.
terms.eli16: A data structure of connected nodes — like a network of cities connected by roads. The basis of social networks and navigation.

terms.definition: A database using graph structures to store relationships between data. Ideal for social networks, recommendation engines, and knowledge graphs. Neo4j is the leading graph database.
terms.eli16: A database designed around relationships — storing connections between things as first-class citizens, perfect for social networks.

terms.definition: Neural networks operating on graph-structured data, learning node and edge representations by aggregating neighborhood information. Used in drug discovery and social networks.
terms.eli16: Neural networks that learn from networked data — like predicting properties of molecules by learning from their atomic graph structure.

terms.definition: Algorithms for visiting all nodes in a graph — breadth-first search (BFS) visits level by level; depth-first search (DFS) follows paths to their end before backtracking.
terms.eli16: Algorithms for visiting every node in a network — BFS spreads outward level by level, DFS plunges deep before backtracking.

terms.definition: Using parallel processing and supercomputers to solve complex problems. Critical for AI model training, scientific simulation, and large-scale data processing.
terms.eli16: Extremely powerful computing using many processors in parallel — essential for training large AI models.

terms.definition: An AI system design where human judgment is incorporated into AI decision-making. Humans review, correct, or approve AI outputs especially for high-stakes decisions.
terms.eli16: AI systems that involve a human reviewer for important decisions — combining AI speed with human judgment.

terms.definition: A high-level search method that selects or generates heuristics rather than directly solving optimization problems. Aims to automate the design of problem-solving strategies.
terms.eli16: An AI that chooses or creates problem-solving heuristics automatically — an algorithm that designs algorithms.

terms.definition: A metric for evaluating the quality and diversity of images generated by generative models, based on how well a pre-trained Inception classifier can classify them.
terms.eli16: A metric for measuring how good AI-generated images are — checking if they're both realistic and varied.

terms.definition: Combining information from multiple heterogeneous sources into a unified, coherent representation. A key challenge in enterprise AI and knowledge management.
terms.eli16: Combining information from many different systems into one consistent view — connecting disparate data sources.

terms.definition: An early AI programming language developed by Newell and Simon in the 1950s, used to write the General Problem Solver. One of the first symbolic AI languages.
terms.eli16: One of the first AI programming languages from the 1950s — used to write some of the earliest symbolic AI programs.

terms.definition: Managing computing infrastructure through machine-readable code files rather than manual processes. Enables reproducible, versioned infrastructure — tools: Terraform, CloudFormation.
terms.eli16: Managing servers and cloud resources using code files instead of manual clicking — making infrastructure reproducible.

terms.definition: Using technology to enhance human intellectual capabilities — helping people think, remember, and reason better. Often contrasted with replacing human intelligence.
terms.eli16: Using technology to make humans smarter and more capable — extending human intelligence rather than replacing it.

terms.definition: Combining RPA with AI — NLP, ML, computer vision — to automate complex, judgment-intensive processes beyond simple rule-based tasks.
terms.eli16: Advanced automation combining robots that follow rules with AI that understands context — automating complex knowledge work.

terms.definition: A platform that provides self-service infrastructure and tooling to development teams, abstracting away complexity so developers can deploy and manage apps without deep infrastructure knowledge.
terms.eli16: An internal toolkit giving developers self-service access to infrastructure — deploy apps without needing IT help.

terms.definition: An early influential knowledge representation language for semantic networks and frames. One of the first description logic systems, developed at BBN Technologies in the 1970s.
terms.eli16: An early AI knowledge representation system from the 1970s that influenced modern ontology languages.

terms.definition: A classification algorithm that predicts the class of a data point based on the majority class of its k nearest neighbors in feature space.
terms.eli16: A simple ML algorithm that classifies something by looking at what its closest neighbors are labeled — majority vote wins.

terms.definition: An AI system using a knowledge base of domain-specific facts and rules to reason and solve problems — the basis of expert systems.
terms.eli16: An AI system that uses encoded expert knowledge and rules to answer questions and solve problems in a specific field.

terms.definition: Building and maintaining knowledge bases for AI systems — eliciting knowledge from experts, formalizing it, and encoding it in a knowledge representation language.
terms.eli16: The work of capturing expert knowledge, formalizing it, and encoding it so AI systems can reason with it.

terms.definition: A computer-oriented language for representing knowledge in first-order logic, designed for exchanging knowledge between different AI systems.
terms.eli16: A standard format for expressing AI knowledge so different systems can share and understand it.

terms.definition: A statistical model assigning probabilities to text sequences. Modern neural language models (LLMs) are the foundation of ChatGPT, Claude, and most AI writing tools.
terms.eli16: An AI model that learns the patterns of language — predicting likely words — the foundation of modern AI text generation.

terms.definition: Reducing words to their base dictionary form. 'Running' → 'run', 'better' → 'good'. Essential NLP preprocessing for text analysis.
terms.eli16: Reducing words to their base form so AI treats different versions of a word as the same — 'running' and 'ran' both become 'run'.

terms.definition: Systematic errors in AI predictions caused by biased training data, flawed model design, or deployment context. Can perpetuate and amplify societal biases.
terms.eli16: When an AI produces unfair results because its training data or design contained human biases.

terms.definition: Two fundamental rules of logical inference. Modus ponens: if P then Q; P is true; therefore Q. Modus tollens: if P then Q; Q is false; therefore P is false.
terms.eli16: Two basic logic rules: modus ponens concludes Q from 'if P then Q' and P being true; modus tollens concludes not-P from Q being false.

terms.definition: A system of multiple interacting AI agents that work together or compete to achieve individual or collective goals. Foundation for simulations and complex AI systems.
terms.eli16: Multiple AI agents working together or competing — each acting independently but interacting toward shared or individual goals.

terms.definition: A feedforward neural network with one or more hidden layers trained with backpropagation. The classic neural network architecture.
terms.eli16: The classic neural network: layers of connected artificial neurons learning by adjusting weights based on errors.

terms.definition: An extension of swarm intelligence optimization where multiple interacting sub-swarms explore a search space simultaneously, improving coverage and avoiding local optima.
terms.eli16: A swarm optimization technique using multiple cooperating groups of agents to explore a solution space more thoroughly.

terms.definition: In genetic algorithms, a random modification applied to a solution to maintain diversity and explore new areas of the search space. Prevents premature convergence.
terms.eli16: A random change in genetic algorithms — prevents all solutions from converging on the same answer by introducing variation.

terms.definition: An approach to natural language understanding using simple, common-sense representations of word meanings — not formal logic but intuitive semantic features.
terms.eli16: A simple approach to AI language understanding using everyday common-sense meaning rather than formal logic.

terms.definition: In programming and AI, the association of a name (identifier or variable) with a value or object. Fundamental to scoping rules and logic programming.
terms.eli16: The process of associating a variable name with a value in programming — the mechanism behind how variables get their values.

terms.definition: An NLP task identifying and classifying named entities in text — people, organizations, locations, dates — into predefined categories.
terms.eli16: AI that reads text and highlights important entities — finding all the names, companies, places, and dates mentioned.

terms.definition: In the Semantic Web, a named graph is an RDF graph paired with a URI that names it, enabling provenance tracking and multiple graphs in one dataset.
terms.eli16: A labeled collection of RDF data in semantic web systems — a named graph can be identified and referenced by its URI.

terms.definition: AI designed to perform a specific task well but unable to generalize beyond its training domain. All current AI systems are narrow AI.
terms.eli16: AI that excels at one specific thing but can't do anything outside that domain — all AI today is narrow AI.

terms.definition: Recurring subgraphs or patterns in networks that appear significantly more often than in random networks. Used to identify functional building blocks in biological and social networks.
terms.eli16: Small recurring patterns in networks that appear more than expected by chance — like identifying common structural motifs in gene regulation networks.

terms.definition: Machine translation using neural networks (particularly transformers) to translate text. Replaced statistical MT and achieves near-human quality for many language pairs.
terms.eli16: AI translation using neural networks — the technology behind modern Google Translate achieving near-human quality.

terms.definition: A neural network augmented with external memory and read/write attention mechanisms, giving it algorithmic capabilities similar to a Turing machine.
terms.eli16: A neural network that can read and write to external memory — making it capable of algorithms that standard neural networks can't do.

terms.definition: The intersection of cybernetics and neuroscience — studying feedback and control mechanisms in nervous systems to inspire AI and neural prosthetics.
terms.eli16: The study of control mechanisms in nervous systems — bridging neuroscience and engineering to understand and replicate brain control.

terms.definition: Computing hardware mimicking the structure of biological neural networks for brain-like efficiency. Intel's Loihi and IBM's TrueNorth are neuromorphic chips.
terms.eli16: Chips designed to work like the human brain — massively parallel and energy-efficient for AI tasks.

terms.definition: A fundamental element in graph theory, neural networks, and distributed systems. In graphs: a vertex in a network. In neural networks: an artificial neuron. In distributed systems: a server in a cluster.
terms.eli16: A basic unit in many computing contexts — a point in a network, an artificial neuron, or a server in a cluster.

terms.definition: An approach to AI pioneered by Rodney Brooks that rejected symbolic AI in favor of building intelligence from simple, reactive behaviors that interact with the real world.
terms.eli16: An approach to AI from the 1980s-90s that built robots from simple reactive behaviors instead of complex symbolic reasoning.

terms.definition: Complexity classes: NP problems are verifiable in polynomial time. NP-complete are the hardest in NP. NP-hard are at least as hard. The P vs NP problem is unsolved.
terms.eli16: Complexity theory classes for hard problems — NP-complete problems have no known fast solution but answers can be quickly verified.

terms.definition: Automated extraction of ontologies (structured knowledge representations) from text corpora, databases, or other sources. Reduces the manual effort of knowledge engineering.
terms.eli16: Automatically building knowledge graphs and ontologies from text — having AI extract structured knowledge from unstructured sources.

terms.definition: AI models and software whose code, weights, or data are publicly available. Examples: Llama, Mistral, Stable Diffusion. Enables community innovation and transparency.
terms.eli16: AI models and tools freely available for anyone to use, modify, or build on — the open-source movement applied to AI.

terms.definition: An open-source AI framework developed by Ben Goertzel aiming for artificial general intelligence. Combines multiple AI paradigms including symbolic AI, probabilistic logic, and neural networks.
terms.eli16: An open-source project aiming to build general AI by combining symbolic reasoning, neural networks, and probabilistic logic.

terms.definition: Technology converting scanned documents, PDFs, and photos into machine-readable text. A key component of document digitization and AI document processing.
terms.eli16: Technology that reads printed text from images and converts it to editable digital text — scanning documents into searchable files.

terms.definition: A technique for reducing the state space in model checking by exploiting the commutativity of concurrent operations — only exploring representative interleavings.
terms.eli16: An optimization for verifying concurrent systems — pruning redundant execution paths where the order doesn't matter.

terms.definition: A framework for decision-making under uncertainty where the agent cannot directly observe the full state of the environment — must maintain a belief state.
terms.eli16: A framework for AI decision-making when the agent can't see the full situation — it must reason from partial information.

terms.definition: An optimization algorithm inspired by bird flocking and fish schooling. Particles move through search space guided by personal best and swarm best positions.
terms.eli16: An optimization algorithm where a swarm of solutions flies through the search space, guided by the best positions found.

terms.definition: A formal logical system extending propositional logic with predicates, quantifiers, and variables. Enables statements about all or some objects. Basis of many AI knowledge representation systems.
terms.eli16: Logic that can make general statements about objects using predicates and quantifiers — more powerful than simple true/false logic.

terms.definition: AI systems analyzing historical data to forecast future outcomes — sales forecasting, churn prediction, equipment failure, demand planning.
terms.eli16: AI that predicts future events based on historical patterns — like forecasting which customers will cancel or when equipment will fail.

terms.definition: A dimensionality reduction technique transforming data into a lower-dimensional space by identifying principal components — directions of maximum variance.
terms.eli16: A technique for simplifying data by finding the most important directions of variation — compressing it while keeping what matters most.

terms.definition: A programming paradigm where programs define probabilistic models. The system handles inference automatically. Examples: Stan, PyMC, Pyro.
terms.eli16: A programming approach for AI that reasons under uncertainty — programs describe what's likely and the system handles the probability math.

terms.definition: The branch of logic dealing with propositions (true/false statements) connected by logical operators (AND, OR, NOT, IF-THEN). The foundation of digital circuits and symbolic AI.
terms.eli16: The logic of true/false statements connected by AND, OR, NOT — the foundation of digital circuits and symbolic AI.

terms.definition: A popular reinforcement learning algorithm that balances learning speed and stability by clipping policy updates. Used to train ChatGPT via RLHF.
terms.eli16: A reinforcement learning algorithm that learns policies stably — the algorithm used to train ChatGPT with human feedback.

terms.definition: The challenge in AI of specifying all the conditions (qualifications) necessary for an action to have its intended effect. Related to the frame problem — real-world actions have infinite preconditions.
terms.eli16: The AI challenge of listing every condition needed for an action to work — in reality, the list is endless.

terms.definition: In logic, a quantifier specifies the quantity of objects a statement applies to. Universal quantifier (∀) means 'for all'; existential quantifier (∃) means 'there exists at least one'.
terms.eli16: Logical symbols that specify scope: ∀ (for all) and ∃ (there exists at least one) — fundamental to mathematical logic and AI reasoning.

terms.definition: Tools for tracking the performance, availability, and behavior of software applications in production. Detects issues, tracks response times, and provides visibility into application health.
terms.eli16: Software that watches your apps in real time — catching slowdowns, errors, and availability issues before users notice.

terms.definition: A technique using LLMs to automatically generate and evaluate prompts for other LLMs, finding optimal instructions without manual engineering.
terms.eli16: AI that automatically writes and tests better prompts for other AI systems — no manual prompt engineering needed.

terms.definition: Google Cloud's fully managed batch computing service for running large-scale parallel workloads. Automatically provisions compute resources for AI training jobs and data processing tasks.
terms.eli16: Google Cloud's service for running large-scale computing jobs in parallel — ideal for AI training and data processing tasks.

terms.definition: Cloud-based customer contact center solutions replacing on-premises call center infrastructure. AI-powered platforms include conversational AI, real-time agent assistance, and analytics.
terms.eli16: Cloud call center technology — replacing physical call center equipment with AI-powered cloud services.

terms.definition: A recurrent neural network architecture with gating mechanisms controlling information flow. More efficient than LSTMs with similar performance on sequence tasks.
terms.eli16: A type of neural network for processing sequences — like LSTM but simpler, using gates to control what information to remember.

terms.definition: A reliability metric measuring average time to restore a system after failure. MTTR = total downtime / number of failures. Key DevOps and SRE performance indicator.
terms.eli16: The average time to fix a broken system — a key measure of how quickly and reliably your team responds to outages.

terms.definition: An automated prompt optimization technique that generates and evaluates multiple candidate instruction sets for LLMs, finding the best-performing prompts systematically.
terms.eli16: An algorithm that automatically discovers the best prompts for AI models by testing many candidates and picking winners.

terms.definition: A deep neural network using residual (skip) connections to allow very deep networks to train effectively. Won ImageNet 2015 and enabled networks with hundreds of layers.
terms.eli16: A neural network that bypasses some layers with shortcut connections — the innovation that made very deep networks trainable.

terms.definition: Security tools aggregating and analyzing log data across IT environments to detect threats in real time. Combines security information management with event correlation.
terms.eli16: Security software that collects logs from all your systems and uses AI to spot threats and suspicious activity in real time.

terms.definition: Technology hosting desktop operating systems on centralized servers. Users access their desktops remotely from any device — AI optimizes performance and resource allocation.
terms.eli16: Your desktop computer running in the cloud — access your full work environment from any device, anywhere.
